## Paper

## Abstract

Non-ionic electronic skins offer intrinsic environmental stability, avoiding the leakage, volatility, and temperature sensitivity that limit ionic sensing systems. Yet, capacitive sensors based on electronic polarization typically exhibit low sensitivity because their dielectric modulation is confined to a single mode. Here, we introduce a dielectric-gradient, fully fiber-integrated non-ionic capacitive architecture that employs an impedance-driven enhancement mechanism. Controlled fiber deformation establishes a dual-variable dielectric network in which pressure-induced reduction of interfacial resistance and impedance releases suppressed polarization, yielding amplified capacitance far beyond that of conventional non-ionic sensors. The resulting device achieves ultrahigh sensitivity of 169.8 kPa-1 over a wide range of 20 Pa–8 MPa and maintains stable operation from −80 °C to 200 °C with less than 6% deviation. When integrated into a tactile-sensing glove and combined with machine learning, it attains 99.25% accuracy in recognizing multiple operational tools under both cryogenic and high-temperature conditions. These findings establish impedance engineering as a universal strategy for constructing high-gain, thermally robust, and reliable non-ionic electronic skins, enabling precision tactile sensing in environments previously inaccessible to flexible electronics.

---

## Introduction

The development of flexible electronic skin is shifting from laboratory demonstrations toward long-term applications in harsh environments1-4. For robotic manipulation, human–machine collaboration at extreme temperatures, and in situ monitoring of critical equipment, sensors must detect weak pressures with high resolution while maintaining stable operation under low and high temperatures and complex mechanical loads. Current progress shows that achieving both high sensitivity and environmental stability remains difficult5-7. This conflict has become a key bottleneck preventing electronic skin from being deployed in real-world scenarios. Notably, recent capacitive and iontronic sensors have already achieved wide pressure ranges and high sensitivities through graded dielectric designs, hierarchical porous architectures, and impedance-engineered interfaces, highlighting the effectiveness of structural design in boosting signal output8-11.

Meanwhile, beyond environmental stability, practical wearable and implantable applications further requires tissue-like conformal contact to maintain long-term signal fidelity on soft and dynamically deforming surfaces. Recent advances in tissue-like wearable and implantable bioelectronics have underscored that long-term signal fidelity critically depends on device structure conformality, such as mechanically compliant, and stable contact with biological tissues. Notable strategies, including conformal nanomembranes12, soft morphing interfaces13, and mechanically matched architectures14,15, which have demonstrated improved bio integration and reduced motion-induced artifacts, enabling more reliable sensing in practical wearable settings. However, integrating tissue-like conformality with wide-temperature robustness and drift-resistant readout under harsh conditions remains nontrivial, especially for sensing schemes in which signal generation relies on mobile-ion transport.

Ionic pressure sensors generate large capacitance variations under small loads through the coupling of ionic migration and interfacial capacitance governed by the electric double layer effect. This mechanism has driven the rapid development of highly sensitive tactile perception in recent years16-18. The physical basis lies in the displacement of mobile ions and the accumulation of interfacial charges, enabling pressure resolution comparable to that of human skin19-21. However, such performance often comes with practical challenges in harsh environments, because ionic systems relying on mobile ions may suffer from leakage, evaporation, and thermal degradation16,22, and their electrical response can exhibit pronounced temperature dependence. At low temperature, ion freezing reduces the response, while at high temperature, excessive activation causes signal drift and mismatch. Even with improved encapsulation or electrolyte formulations, the temperature dependence and possible phase transitions of ionic transport remain difficult to eliminate. As a result, maintaining reliable operation across a wide temperature range is still unrealistic23,24.

Non-ionic capacitive sensors rely on electronic polarization rather than ionic conduction and therefore possess superior material stability, thermal endurance, and encapsulation compatibility7,25-27. Extensive research has focused on enhancing their dielectric constants and structural compliance. Reported strategies include incorporating high-permittivity fillers, constructing porous or microstructure layers, and designing multilayer or gradient geometries to improve stress transfer28,29. These approaches have enhanced low-pressure responses and extended the detectable range to some extent, but they have not fundamentally broken through the sensitivity ceiling of non-ionic systems30,31. The limited polarizable volume and modest enhancement of the effective electric field make it difficult to balance initial capacitance and noise. As pressure increases, contact rearrangement gradually saturates, and the signal gain reaches a plateau with reduced linearity. Most current methods rely on geometric or single dielectric-channel amplification and fail to address the key impedance factors that suppress polarization in non-ionic systems32-34.

The measured capacitance of non-ionic sensors depends not only on the number of polarizable dipoles and the effective contact area but also on the suppression of polarization caused by series impedance. Incomplete interfacial contact, dielectric losses, and local high resistance in the electrode network jointly determine the polarization time scale through the equivalent series resistance and the operating frequency, which lowers the apparent capacitance within the working range17,35,36. Such suppressed polarization, often overlooked in conventional geometric optimization, prevents materials with high intrinsic polarizability from expressing their full response potential. The existence of this impedance-induced suppression indicates that the performance limitation of non-ionic sensors originates not from insufficient dielectric modulation but from the lack of a mechanism that can release the constrained polarization under operating conditions37.

To address this issue, we introduce a dielectric-gradient all-fiber capacitive architecture that enables impedance-driven capacitance enhancement. In this design, a cooperative network composed of highly conductive electrode fibers and low-conductive dielectric fibers, together with pressure-induced fiber rearrangement, reduces interfacial impedance and activates dipole polarization simultaneously. The combined effects of decreased impedance suppression and expanded polarizable volume create a synergistic amplification of the capacitive signal. Frequency-domain analysis reveals a clear transition from resistive-dominant to capacitive-dominant behavior, while finite-element simulations and microscopic observations confirm pressure-induced interfacial reconstruction and the formation of new dielectric pathways. The resulting sensor achieves a high sensitivity of 169.84 kPa⁻¹, a broad detection range from 20 Pa to 8 MPa, and stable performance between −80 °C and 200 °C with less than six percent deviation. When integrated into a machine-learning-assisted tactile glove, it attains an object-recognition accuracy of 99.25 percent even under extreme temperature conditions. This impedance-driven amplification mechanism provides a new pathway for non-ionic systems to achieve iontronic-level sensitivity while maintaining environmental robustness, and it establishes a general framework for reliable flexible tactile sensing in complex and demanding environments.

---

## Results

2.1 Impedance-driven capacitive sensing design

Flexible capacitive pressure sensors can generally be divided into non-ionic and ionic types according to their signal transduction mechanisms (Supplementary Figure S1). Ionic sensors exploit the migration of mobile ions and the formation of electric double layers (EDLs), which yield large capacitance variations under small stimuli but suffer from leakage and strong temperature dependence. Non-ionic sensors, in contrast, rely on electronic polarization within solid dielectrics, providing better environmental stability but limited capacitance change because their output originates solely from minor variations of geometry and permittivity. Bridging the advantages of both mechanisms requires a non-ionic strategy that can internally amplify the polarization response without relying on ion transport.

The sensitivity of a capacitive sensor is given by

S = 1/C0 * dCmeas/dP (1)

where C0 is the initial capacitance and Cmeas the measured capacitance at angular frequency ω. For non-ionic systems, the equivalent impedance model can be expressed as

Z(ω,P) = Rs(P) + 1/(jωCs(ω,P)) (2)

where Rs(P) denotes the pressure-dependent series resistance and Cs(ω,P) the apparent capacitance of the dielectric structure. The measurable capacitance can then be expressed as

Cmeas = Cs(ω,P) = Cgeo(P) + Cpol(P)Φ(ω/ωtr(P)) (3)

Here, Cgeo(P) is the geometric capacitance governed by the electrode contact area and dielectric thickness, Cpol(P) is the dipolar polarization capacitance determined by the density of polarizable domains and interfacial junctions, and Φ(ω/ωtr) is a dispersive factor representing the ability of polarization to follow the alternating field. The transition frequency ωtr(P) is inversely proportional to the product Rs(P)Cs(P) and increases as pressure reduces Rs(P).

Differentiating equation with respect to pressure yields

dCmeas/dP = dCgeo/dP + dCpol/dP * Φ + Cpol * dΦ/dωtr * dωtr/dP (4)

geo. contribution pol. contribution impedance contribution

This expression indicates that the measurable capacitance change originates from three cooperative contributions. The geometric contribution arises from pressure-induced densification that increases the effective contact area and decreases the dielectric spacing, thereby raising Cgeo. The polarization contribution stems from the formation of new interfacial junctions and enhanced dipole alignment, which elevate Cpol. The impedance-release contribution originates from the reduction of Rs(P), which shifts ωtr toward higher frequencies and allows a greater fraction of dipoles to respond to the alternating field, thus amplifying the capacitance.

From Equations above, achieving high sensitivity requires a design that maximizes the pressure-induced capacitance change dCmeas/dP while minimizing the initial capacitance C0. This can be realized by simultaneously strengthening the effects of structural densification and polarization activation, and by promoting efficient impedance release. A porous architecture with compressible dielectric domains can enlarge the variation of Cgeo, a heterogeneous dielectric composition can enhance RCs through increased polarizable interfaces, and a conductive network with moderate resistance can enable a strong pressure dependence of Rs(P). Balancing these three factors yields a structure capable of converting mechanical compression into a pronounced electrical response without relying on ionic transport. The combined influence of these mechanisms establishes the general physical foundation for impedance-driven capacitance amplification and provides the theoretical guidance for designing high-sensitivity non-ionic capacitive sensors.

Guided by the theoretical analysis, we constructed a dielectric-gradient all-fiber capacitive architecture that translates pressure-induced impedance modulation into a measurable capacitance amplification (Figure 1a). At zero load, the highly porous network and limited inter-fiber contact produce a large initial series resistance Rs(0) and a small baseline capacitance C0. When external pressure is applied, the effective contact area (Aed) increases rapidly, the fraction of polarizable volume expands, and the previously constrained dipoles are released, leading to a substantial increase in capacitance (ΔC). This reversible transition from a resistive-dominant to a polarization-active regime constitutes the fundamental working principle of the impedance-driven response, as analytically described in Supplementary Note 1.

In the series-readout representation, the device response can be described by an effective series resistance Rs in series with an effective storage capacitance Cs, such that the capacitance reported by the LCR meter is an impedance-derived apparent capacitance rather than a purely geometric capacitance. Whether this storage component can be expressed within a given AC measurement window is governed by the electrical relaxation time of the series branch, τ ∼ RsCs, which defines a characteristic (transition) frequency

ωtr ≈ 1/τ ≈ 1/(RsCs) (f = ωtr/2π) (5)

A larger Rs leads to a longer τ, thereby constraining polarization-related charge storage at a fixed test frequency, whereas a reduced Rs shortens τ and shifts ωtr to higher frequency, making a larger fraction of the storage response observable. In this context, impedance release refers to the pressure-induced decrease of Rs, which increases ωtr and enables an enhanced apparent capacitive output under the same AC readout conditions; the frequency-domain evidence for this shift is discussed in following text.

The sensor structure comprises alternately stacked conductive and dielectric fiber layers with a precisely tuned carbon nanotube (CNTs) concentration gradient (Figure 1b and Supplementary Figure S2). These layers were fabricated through an airflow-spinning process under identical processing conditions, followed by thermal imidization of poly(amic acid) into polyimide (PI) with excellent temperature resistance (Supplementary Figures S3 and S4), with a structural porosity of up to 90%, estimated using a density-based method (Supplementary Table S1). Notably, the millimeter-scale device thickness (~2 mm; inset of Figure 1b) is not dictated by uncontrolled fiber stacking, but is defined during thermal imidization using a fixed 2 mm mold cavity, ensuring good thickness reproducibility across samples (Supplementary Figure S5). Meanwhile, the device is intended to operate within the thermal endurance window of the PI/CNT system, while direct flame exposure beyond this limit may induce irreversible decomposition/carbonization and unstable signals (Supplementary Figure S6). Cross-sectional SEM observations reveal well-interpenetrated interfaces that maintain mechanical continuity and facilitate stress transfer across layers (Figure 1c and Supplementary Figure S7). Individual fiber cross-sections show that the CNTs are densely distributed within the electrode layer and sparsely, yet uniformly, dispersed within the dielectric layer (Figure 1d and Supplementary Figure S8), forming a conductivity–permittivity gradient that enables continuous tuning of Rs(P) under compression. Importantly, the differences between the electrode and dielectric fibers are caused by the content of CNTs in the spinning dope, whereas the airflow-spinning conditions were kept identical for all layers, helping minimize processing-induced variability and improve diameter uniformity and reproducibility (Supplementary Figure S5). As the structure is compressed, the porous network gradually densifies and new inter-fiber junctions emerge (Figure 1e). Kelvin probe force microscopy reveals a distinct potential contrast at the inter-fiber junctions, where the local surface potential increases from approximately 173 mV on isolated fibers to about 196 mV at overlapping regions (Figure 1f and Supplementary Figure S9). This potential elevation indicates enhanced charge accumulation and local dipole activation at the newly formed contacts, directly confirming the creation of additional dielectric pathways that substantiate the predicted impedance-release mechanism. Consistently, additional multi-site KPFM mappings and conductive-AFM measurements further support junction-enabled conduction within the dielectric network under compression (Supplementary Fig. S9).

The PI matrix endows the all-fiber architecture with high stiffness, excellent thermal stability, and reversible deformation capability, thereby maintaining interfacial integrity during repeated compression. The electrode and dielectric fiber mats exhibit tensile strengths of approximately 115 MPa and 70 MPa and moduli of 6.3 GPa and 4.9 GPa, respectively (Supplementary Figure S10), ensuring efficient load transfer and structural stability throughout the full pressure range. The compressive stress–strain response (Figure 1g) displays pronounced strain hardening, arising from progressive pore collapse and inter-fiber contact densification, which enables continuous impedance modulation without structural failure. Collectively, these results confirm that the hierarchical fiber network provides a robust mechanical foundation for the impedance-driven capacitive sensing concept, transforming the theoretical design framework into a practical and reliable structural embodiment.

2.2 Sensing mechanism and performance

The impedance-driven mechanism proposed above was experimentally verified through frequency-domain analysis, compositional tuning, and structural modeling. The impedance–frequency map (Figure 2a and Supplementary Figure S11) divides the sensor’s behavior into three regions characterized by ωRsCs: the resistive-dominant regime (ωRsCs > 10), the transition regime (0.1 < ωRsCs < 10), and the capacitive-dominant regime (ωRsCs < 0.1). At 0 kPa, the device lies in the transition regime, and increasing pressure enhances electronic conduction in the CNTs network and reduces Rs, progressively relaxing the resistive constraint. Accordingly, the extracted Cs is an impedance-derived apparent capacitance, for which a lower Rs makes polarization-related storage increasingly accessible at the measurement frequency.

The frequency evolution of the impedance imaginary component provides a spectral signature of this shift (Figure 2b). Here, |X| denotes the magnitude of the imaginary impedance. At 0 kPa, |X| exhibits a weak maximum within the measurable window (102–105 Hz), whereas at higher pressures (200–8000 kPa), it shows no discernible peak across the same range. This monotonic increase indicates that the relaxation peak has shifted beyond the measurement band as pressure rises, consistent with a decrease in Rs and a corresponding increase in the characteristic frequency ωtr. Thus, pressure accelerates the polarization dynamics and converts the system from a resistive-dominated state to a polarization-active state, in agreement with the theoretical criterion derived in Supplementary Note 1.

To quantitatively differentiate conduction-dominated artifacts from polarization-related loss, we performed broadband dielectric spectroscopy of the full device under representative compressive strains (0, 50, and 80%). The measured imaginary permittivity ε''(ω) was decomposed into a conduction term (ε''cond(ω)) and a polarization-loss term (ε''pol(ω)) according to

ε''(ω) = ε''pol(ω) + ε''cond(ω), ε''cond(ω) = σ'(ω)/(ε0ω) (6)

where σ'(ω) is the real part of AC conductivity, ε0 is the vacuum dielectric constant (ε0 ≈ 8.854×10−12 F/m). Notably, across the measured frequency range and for all strains, the conduction contribution ε''cond(ω) remains about two orders of magnitude smaller than ε''pol(ω) over most of the measured frequency range, indicating that the imaginary permittivity is dominated by polarization-related dissipation rather than pure conduction leakage. Meanwhile, compression increases σ'(ω) (consistent with enhanced conductive pathways and loss), but ε''pol(ω) remains the main component and evolves systematically with strain, supporting that the capacitance amplification is not solely a leakage-driven artifact (Supplementary Figure S12).

At a fixed readout frequency of 10 kHz, both the series resistance Rs (left axis) and the imaginary component |X| (right axis) decrease markedly with increasing pressure (Figure 2c). Under the series-equivalent readout and within the transition-to-capacitive regime, the concurrent reduction of Rs and |X| is consistent with an increase in the extracted series capacitance Cs at the same measurement frequency. This behavior reflects a pressure-induced shift of the readout window governed by ωCsRs through which polarization-related responses become increasingly accessible in the AC measurement. In this sense, the observed impedance-controlled capacitance amplification represents the experimental manifestation of the pressure-dependent polarization term Cpol(P)Φ(ω/ωtr(P)), as formalized in the impedance-release model in Supplementary Note 1.

Notably, the capacitance enhancement is not uniquely tied to mechanical compression. To decouple impedance modulation from deformation, two zero-pressure control experiments were conducted (Supplementary Figure S13). First, with the electrode CNTs loading fixed at 20 wt.%, increasing the dielectric CNTs content (6–11 wt.%) monotonically reduced Rs and increased the extracted Cs. Second, introducing external series resistors (100 Ω–1 MΩ) systematically suppressed the measured Cs. Together, these results demonstrate that the enhanced impedance-derived apparent capacitance is governed by the total series resistance within the AC readout window, while mechanical compression mainly serves as a convenient and reversible means to reduce Rs in a single device.

The compositional dependence of the two fiber layers defines the effective impedance window of the sensor. When the dielectric layer (9 wt.% CNTs) was paired with electrode layers containing 18–20 wt.% CNTs, the capacitance–pressure (ΔC/C0) curves exhibited a two-region linear response (Figure 2d). The first region corresponds to impedance release at low pressures, while the second originates from cooperative growth of polarization and contact area at higher pressures. Figure 2e shows the enlarged sensitivity map in the low-pressure range, highlighting the corresponding sensitivity differences. Moreover, the sensor response is highly reproducible across three independently fabricated batches (<6% variation in sensitivity; Supplementary Figure S14). Over-doping the dielectric layer (10 wt.% CNTs) led to signal distortion and loss of capacitance response above ~5 MPa (Supplementary Figure S15), whereas replacing the porous electrode with a metallic foil increased C0 to ~8 nF and induced inductive behavior at ~7 MPa. Importantly, because the Cu foil electrode presents a dense and continuous conductive surface, extensive interfacial contact with the dielectric layer is already established in the initial state, resulting in a high baseline capacitance (C0). This significantly reduces the relative capacitance change (ΔC/C0) and limits the achievable sensitivity. In contrast, the porous fiber electrode exhibits restricted initial contact and higher interfacial impedance, allowing polarization to be gradually activated under applied pressure. This enables a wider dynamic modulation range of the series impedance and leads to a more effective and stable capacitance readout (Supplementary Figure S16). These results confirm that the impedance-tunable, porous architecture is essential for maintaining capacitive operation across a wide pressure range. Pressure-dependent resistances of the electrode Re(P) and dielectric Rd(P) layers reveal the same trend, both decreasing by several orders of magnitude as the structure compresses (Figure 2f). This evolution provides direct experimental evidence for Equation (S2) in Supplementary Note 1, where pressure-induced enlargement of contact area Acontact(P) and reduction in resistive path length jointly lower Rs(P) = Re + Rd.

Finite-element analysis (FEA) provides further insight into the cooperative contributions of the electrode and dielectric layers (Figures 2g and h; Supplementary Figures S17 and S18). When deformation occurs only in the dielectric layer (model D) or only in the electrode layer (model E), the simulated capacitance–pressure response C(P) increases only slightly. In contrast, the coupled deformation model (E–D) accurately reproduces the experimentally observed two-slope behavior. This result demonstrates that geometric densification and impedance modulation operate in concert, where mechanical compression simultaneously lowers Rs and enhances Cs, ultimately yielding the pronounced capacitance amplification observed in the impedance-driven sensor.

The impedance-driven all-fiber sensor demonstrates a combination of ultrahigh sensitivity and remarkable mechanical resilience. In the sensitivity–pressure diagram (Figure 2i and Supplementary Table S2), the sensor occupies the high-sensitivity and wide-pressure-range quadrant, surpassing conventional non-ionic capacitive sensors and approaching the response levels of ionic counterparts4,7,16,19,26,29,31,40-43. It delivers a maximum sensitivity of 169.8 kPa-1 within a broad range up to 8 MPa, together with an ultralow detection limit of approximately 20 Pa (Supplementary Figure S19). In addition, representative loading–unloading curves were measured to quantify hysteresis. The porous fiber network exhibits a stable and reproducible hysteresis loop with closely overlapped responses over successive cycles Within the sensing range of 8MPa (Supplementary Figure S20). The sensor also exhibits rapid polarization–depolarization kinetics, achieving response and recovery times of 5.8 ms and 6.1 ms, respectively (Supplementary Figure S21). To complement the sub-10 ms response/recovery results, we further evaluated loading-rate dependence (10–100 mm min⁻¹) and dwell-time stability at 2000 kPa for 1 h. The sensor maintained consistent robust signal tracking with minimal drift over the holding period (Supplementary Fig. S22). Meanwhile, under repetitive loading at 2 MPa, the device maintains a stable capacitance output for more than 20 000 cycles without observable baseline drift (Figure 2j), confirming excellent structural reversibility and long-term operational reliability.

2.3 Temperature-independent sensing performance

Building upon the impedance-driven design and structural validation described above, the environmental stability of the all-fiber sensor was further evaluated under extreme temperature conditions. For high-performance tactile sensors, temperature represents a critical factor that often limits practical deployment. In ionic and hybrid iontronic systems, the electrical activity of mobile ions is inherently temperature-dependent, leading to pronounced signal fluctuations over broad temperature ranges. At subzero temperatures, ionic motion is severely restricted, resulting in functional degradation, whereas at elevated temperatures, excessive ion mobility causes anomalous signal amplification and drift (Supplementary Figure S23). Although conventional non-ionic capacitive sensors exhibit better thermal stability, their low dielectric tunability results in weak sensitivity and limited resolution, hindering high-precision sensing applications under variable thermal environments.

In contrast, the impedance-driven all-fiber sensor demonstrates remarkable signal uniformity and stability across an ultrawide temperature window from −80 °C to 200 °C, enabled by the thermally robust PI matrix, the stable CNTs network, and the low-impedance sensing mechanism. Even under extreme conditions, the device maintains high sensitivities of 165.2 kPa-1 (R2 = 0.9998) at −80 °C and 179.7 kPa⁻¹ (R2 = 0.9997) at 200 °C, with less than 6% deviation, while preserving a broad operating range up to 8 MPa (Figure 3a). Notably, the temperature-invariant normalized response (ΔC/C0) cannot be attributed to the thermally robust PI matrix alone; it also benefits from the low-impedance sensing mechanism. This outstanding temperature-independent performance arises from the coupled mechanical–electrical stability of the fibrous network, where the PI framework maintains structural integrity while the impedance-regulated readout stabilizes the electrical response. To clarify this point, we compared three sensors with the same PI-based architecture, including the impedance-driven PI/CNT device, a conventional capacitive PI device, and an iontronic PI/IL device (Supplementary Figure S24), which show markedly different capacitance responses at elevated temperature, confirming that the robustness is not solely a matrix effect. As shown in Figure 3b, the compressive stress–strain responses measured at −80 °C, 25 °C, and 200 °C exhibit nearly identical modulus values (20 kPa–32 MPa), confirming that the load transfer and deformation behavior remain consistent across the full temperature range.

The electrical characteristics of the CNTs network also contribute to this robustness. The conductivity of CNTs increases nearly proportionally with temperature, which simultaneously enhances both the baseline capacitance C0 and the saturation capacitance, thereby preserving the relative variation ΔC/C0 (Supplementary Figure S25 and Table S3). To further verify robustness against extreme temperature transitions, we performed repeated thermal cycling among −80 °C, 25 °C, and 200 °C, together with multi-level loading–unloading tests from 100 to 2000 kPa. As shown in Figure 3c and Supplementary Figure S26, ΔC/C0, Rs, and tanδ remain highly repeatable throughout successive temperature cycles. Together with the long-term loading and hysteresis characterization, these results confirm stable and reliable sensing under repeated thermal transitions. Long-term durability tests under 2 MPa loading further confirm that the capacitance waveform remains nearly unchanged after 500 cycles at −80 °C and 200 °C (Figures 3d and e), reflecting excellent structural reversibility and environmental endurance.

A quantitative comparison of key performance metrics (Figure 3f and Supplementary Table S4) highlights the distinct advantages of the impedance-driven architecture4,14-16,42,43. The all-fiber sensor achieves a balanced combination of high sensitivity, broad sensing range, and long-term reliability, while maintaining temperature-independent operation across an ultrawide thermal window. This convergence of electrical, mechanical, and environmental robustness resolves the long-standing trade-off that has limited non-ionic capacitive sensors, positioning the device performance on par with or beyond ionic systems. The results confirm that the impedance-driven amplification mechanism not only enhances sensitivity through coordinated modulation of Cs and Rs but also inherently suppresses thermally induced drift, enabling stable signal output under extreme conditions. Such coupling between mechanism-level control and materials-level stability provides a generalizable route toward reliable tactile sensing in harsh environments and paves the way for system-level integration under real-world thermal variations.

2.4 Application demonstration of wide-temperature tactile-sensing gloves

Following the validation of temperature-independent sensing characteristics, the practical applicability of the impedance-driven all-fiber sensor was further verified through a tactile-assistive glove that functions reliably across extreme thermal environments. The concept of this wide-temperature tactile-sensing application is illustrated in Figure 4a, which depicts representative scenarios including high-temperature manufacturing, firefighting, cryogenic operations, and polar or deep-sea exploration. In these real industrial and scientific settings, workers must rely on heavy protective gear for thermal insulation. Although such gloves provide effective temperature protection, their multilayered structure substantially diminishes tactile sensitivity, making precise manipulation more difficult and increasing the likelihood of delayed responses or accidental injuries44-46.

To address these challenges, a wide-temperature tactile-sensing glove was constructed by integrating fourteen all-fiber capacitive pressure sensors into a commercial heat-resistant glove (Figure 4b). The sensors were distributed over the fingertip regions, and the Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) conductive wires were woven between inner layers to maintain flexibility and ensure user comfort. This design allows the glove to provide real-time signal response on grasping pressure and contact conditions while preserving natural motion under both high and low temperatures.

The glove was evaluated under two representative thermal extremes. As shown in Figure 4c, at approximately 200 °C, a wearer grasped and released a heated glass beaker inside a thermal chamber. The glove produced stable, reversible ΔC/C0 responses accompanied by synchronized pressure-distribution maps that clearly reflected the sequence of initial contact, grasping, and release. Under cryogenic conditions near −50 °C, the same glove exhibited equally stable responses while grasping a beaker containing liquid nitrogen (Figure 4d). In both tests, the signal waveforms and thermal–pressure mappings remained consistent, confirming that the tactile-assistive glove delivers reliable and stable tactile signal responses, supporting consistent tactile perception in thermally insulated environments.

Beyond temperature adaptability, the glove was further tested under complex contact modes simulating realistic grasping scenarios. During object manipulation, irregular geometries such as corners, edges, or flat surfaces produce localized stress concentrations that challenge the durability and dynamic range of flexible sensors. Based on an average adult grasping force of ~30 N applied over a 49 mm2 area, the estimated maximum stresses reach approximately 600 kPa for area contact (7 mm × 7 mm), 2.2 MPa for line contact (2 mm × 7 mm), and 7.5 MPa for point contact (2 mm × 2 mm) (Figure 4e). These values exceed the operational limits of most reported flexible sensors but remain well within the 20 Pa–8 MPa range of our impedance-driven architecture. Figure 4f displays the capacitance responses from the thumb sensor while grasping an irregular stone, where distinct and repeatable ΔC/C0 patterns were recorded during sequential transitions from point to line to area contact. This capability confirms that the all-fiber sensors accurately perceive stress distribution and contact modality even under high localized pressure.

These demonstrations confirm that the impedance-driven all-fiber sensors effectively bridge the gap between material design and functional implementation. By maintaining stable and high-fidelity signal outputs under wide-ranging thermal and mechanical conditions, the tactile glove validates the scalability and robustness of the proposed sensing strategy. This system-level demonstration illustrates how impedance modulation can be harnessed to achieve reliable and adaptive tactile perception, establishing a foundation for future intelligent protective systems and robotic interfaces capable of operating in extreme environments.

2.5 Tactile perception and recognition performance

Considering that thick protective clothing in extreme environments can restrict vision and hinder precise control, a multi-object recognition system was developed by combining high-resolution pressure mapping with a two-dimensional convolutional neural network (2D-CNN) (Figure 5a). The system consists of signal acquisition, data preprocessing, and deep-learning recognition modules, operating in conjunction with the tactile-assistive glove to provide real-time signal response on grasping forces and object identification across a wide temperature range. Here, machine learning is used to analyze the pressure-mapping signals captured by our sensor and evaluate the separability of different object patterns47,48. Supplementary Figure S27 presents a simplified workflow of the learning process. Briefly, the raw capacitance signals were converted to normalized relative responses (ΔC/C0), and statistical features (mean and variance) were extracted and reorganized according to the spatial layout of the sensing channels to form 2D input maps. The resulting feature maps were interpolated to a unified 52×52 grid and fed into a 2D-CNN consisting of two convolution–pooling blocks.

To evaluate the comprehensive sensing performance of the impedance-driven all-fiber sensors, two additional reference sensors were prepared for comparison. An iontronic sensor incorporating 50 wt.% ionic liquid in the dielectric layer represented the ionic type, and a pure PI-fiber sensor represented the traditional capacitive type. In a simulated environment containing four representative object shapes including sphere, cube, cylinder, and triangular prism, tactile-response maps were collected at −70 °C, 25 °C, and 200 °C (Figure 5b). In total, 300 pressure-distribution maps were extracted from 30 repeated grasping trials (10 trials at each temperature) during the stable holding stage. To assess trial-to-trial consistency, we take sphere grasping as a representative case and compute the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) between the thumb-tip capacitance signal and a grasping-load proxy estimated from the multi-channel sensor array outputs during the holding stage49. The trial-to-trial variation of the estimated grasping force was within 60 kPa for all three sensor types, and the impedance-driven sensor exhibited a PCC of ~0.8, indicating strong and reproducible force–signal coupling (Supplementary Figure S28). The datasets for the iontronic and traditional sensors are provided in Supplementary Figure S29. Unless otherwise noted, all pressure-distribution maps are displayed using a unified legend referenced to the high-temperature signal range for cross-temperature comparison.

Meanwhile, to improve evaluation robustness, we adopted K-fold cross-validation by dividing the augmented dataset into 6 subsets, using one subset as the non-overlapping test set and the remaining subsets as the training set. Data augmentation was applied to the training folds only to avoid data leakage. This procedure was repeated across 5 folds and the averaged accuracy was reported (Figure 5c-e). The iontronic sensor exhibited strong temperature dependence, performing well at 200 °C but losing functionality at −70 °C because of frozen ionic mobility. Its recognition accuracy was limited to 60.25%. The traditional capacitive sensor maintained consistent output across temperatures owing to its intrinsic thermal stability but produced weak signal intensity and low contrast between objects, resulting in an accuracy of 85.5%. In contrast, the impedance-driven all-fiber sensor maintained consistent relative sensitivity across the entire temperature range. The pressure-mapping patterns of identical objects remained almost unchanged from −70 °C to 200 °C, as indicated by the consistent color scale in Figure 5b. This stability enabled the CNN model to reach a recognition accuracy of 99.25%, representing a substantial improvement over the other two systems.

The high recognition accuracy originates from the stable and high-fidelity pressure signal responses provided by the impedance-driven all-fiber sensors. This stability allows the CNN model to reliably capture subtle differences in pressure distribution caused by variations in object shape, even under extreme temperature conditions. The consistent sensing behavior and strong signal contrast demonstrate that the impedance-driven architecture ensures dependable data quality for tactile perception, confirming the robustness of the sensing mechanism and its suitability for complex, temperature-variable environments.

## Methods

Preparation of Spinning Precursor Solution and Fabrication of Fiber Layers: First, 0.1 g of polyethylene oxide (PEO) was dissolved in 10 g of N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF) under magnetic stirring at room temperature for 1 h to obtain a spinnability-enhancing assistant solution. The incorporation of PEO was intended to improve the fiber-forming ability and homogeneity of the dielectric fibers. Subsequently, precursor spinning solutions for the electrode and dielectric layers were prepared separately: 2 g of the assistant solution was added into 2 g of polyamide acid (PAA) solution, followed by the addition of 0.9 g of CNTs dispersion (H-CNT) and 0.405 g of CNTs dispersion (L-CNT), respectively, to obtain the electrode-layer and dielectric-layer precursor solutions.

The porous fiber sponges were fabricated via a sequential airflow-spinning process. Unless otherwise specified, all three layers were deposited under the same spinning window, and the CNTs loading was the only intentional variable between the electrode and dielectric layers. Specifically, the precursor solution was delivered from a 1 mL syringe through a 30G nozzle (The inner diameter is about 160 μm) at 2 mL h⁻¹, while compressed air at 69 kPa (air velocity ~21 m/s at the nozzle exit) was heated to 80 °C and applied coaxially; the collection distance was 30 cm and each layer was collected for 15 min. After sequential deposition of the bottom electrode, dielectric, and top electrode layers, the stack was thermally imidized and hot-pressed in a fixed 2 mm mold cavity, which defines the final device thickness and improves layer-to-layer uniformity.

The collected fiber sponges were subsequently dried in an oven at 100 ℃ for 1 h to remove residual solvents. Finally, the samples were placed in a fixed-thickness mold and subjected to a stepwise thermal imidization process in a muffle furnace at 100 ℃ for 1 h, 200 ℃ for 1 h, and 300 ℃ for 1 h. This stepwise spinning and imidization strategy enabled the fabrication of a well-integrated three-layer porous fiber architecture (electrode–dielectric–electrode), serving as the basis of the full fiber flexible pressure sensor. The size of the sensor can be customized using a cutter.

Finite Element Analysis: Finite-element simulations were performed using COMSOL Multiphysics. The highly porous (>90%) PI/CNT fibrous architecture was represented in a homogenized manner: instead of explicitly constructing macroscopic pores in the geometry, the porosity of each layer was incorporated through COMSOL’s porous-media representation, in which porosity is treated as an internal model parameter. Mechanical parameters for the electrode and dielectric layers were assigned based on the experimentally measured compressive stress–strain responses of the corresponding layers. Electrical material parameters of the three-layer structure were defined consistently with the experimentally measured layer-wise electrical characteristics and updated according to the measured pressure-dependent resistance evolution of each layer.

The deformation of the layered structure under applied pressure was solved using the Solid Mechanics module. A uniform pressure load was applied on the top surface, while the bottom surface was constrained (Uz = 0). Contact interfaces between layers were assumed to be ideal (frictionless and non-penetrative) to simplify interfacial coupling in the integrated model. The computed deformed configurations were then used as input for the electrical simulations.

The complex impedance response was computed using the AC/DC module under small-signal AC excitation. For electrical boundary conditions, the bottom surface of the model was grounded, while a voltage boundary was applied to the top surface. The overall impedance of the three-layer architecture was extracted, with both real and imaginary components calculated as a function of applied pressure. These results were used to support a trend-level analysis of the impedance-driven capacitive enhancement behavior in the proposed sensor structure.

Mechanical characterization: The mechanical performance of the sensor was systematically characterized using a mechanical testing system (XLD-1000E, Guangzhou Jingkong Testing Co., Ltd.). For the tensile strength measurements, electrode and dielectric layer samples with dimensions of 5 mm × 30 mm were subjected to uniaxial tensile testing at a speed of 50 mm·min⁻¹ until fracture. The corresponding stress–strain curves were recorded to evaluate the tensile strength and Young’s modulus. For the compression tests, samples with dimensions of 7 mm × 7 mm were placed on the compression stage in contact with a flat surface indenter. The indenter was programmed to compress the samples at a constant speed of 5 mm·min⁻¹ until the target strain was reached. This allowed the evaluation of compressive stress and modulus as a core parameter.

Sensitivity and Sensing Performance Measurements: The sensitivity and sensing characteristics of the sensor were characterized using a mechanical testing system (XLD-1000E, Guangzhou Jingkong Testing Co., Ltd.). The sensor samples with dimensions of 7 mm × 7 mm were placed on the testing platform, and a flat indenter was programmed to approach the sample at a controlled rate to apply external forces. During the loading process, the capacitance signals were continuously recorded in real time using an LCR meter (TH2840B, Tonghui Electronics Co., Ltd.) at a fixed test frequency of 10 kHz. For determining the LOD, the sensor was subjected to a gradually increasing programmed gradient force. The minimum force at which a detectable capacitance peak first appeared was defined as the LOD. For response and recovery time measurements, a weight was rapidly placed onto and released from the sensor surface, producing an instantaneous pressure. After maintaining the load for 2 s, the weight was removed. The transient capacitance response and recovery curves were recorded to evaluate the dynamic sensing performance.

Cyclic Durability Testing: To evaluate the stability of the sensor under extreme temperature and high-pressure cyclic conditions, a mechanical testing system equipped with a temperature-controlled environmental chamber and a computer-controlled platform (EUT4000, Shenzhen Sansi Testing Co., Ltd.) was employed. Sensor samples with dimensions of 7 mm × 7 mm were mounted on the testing stage. During the measurements, the target temperature was set and maintained via the environmental chamber. A compressive load was then applied at a controlled rate of 2 mm·min⁻¹ until the sensor was subjected to a pressure of 2000 kPa. Under this condition, high-cycle reciprocating displacement tests were performed to simulate long-term operational stresses. Throughout the cyclic loading process, the capacitance signals of the sensor were continuously recorded in real time using an LCR meter, enabling the evaluation of its signal stability and durability across different temperature environments and under high-pressure cyclic stresses.

Porosity of the sensor: Porosity was estimated using a density-based method. The apparent density of the porous sample (ρapp) was calculated from the measured mass m and geometric volume V. The theoretical density of the solid matrix (ρ0) was taken as 1.47 g/cm3. The porosity P was then calculated as:

P = (1 - ρapp/ρ0) × 100% (7)

Measurements were performed on at least three independent samples and averaged.

Integration and signal acquisition of sensing gloves: Firstly, use a precision cutting tool to cut the flexible pressure sensor into a standard sample of 7 mm × 7 mm. Then use conductive silver paste to bond PTFE high-temperature resistant wires to the top and bottom electrodes of each sample, ensuring reliable electrical connection and thermal stability. In order to integrate with gloves, the sensor is fixed in the designated position using PI double-sided tape, and PI tape is used as a protective surface layer to prevent mechanical wear or environmental damage. The PTFE wire is woven and placed inside the glove to minimize interference with user comfort and operational flexibility. During the testing process, a multi-channel LCR meter (TH2840NX, Tonghui Electronics Co., Ltd.) was used to collect sensing signals in real time at a working frequency of 10kHz, thereby achieving simultaneous monitoring and accurate data acquisition of multiple sensors.

Characterization: A comprehensive set of characterization techniques was employed to investigate the structural and functional properties of the fabricated flexible pressure sensors. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, Zeiss Sigma 300, Germany) was used to observe the microstructure of the fiber networks and interfacial morphologies, highlighting fiber junctions and porosity evolution. Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM, Bruker Dimension ICON, USA) was conducted to map the surface potential distribution at fiber junctions, thereby revealing localized charge accumulation and the formation of new dielectric pathways. Additionally, transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Tecnai F20, USA) was used to examine the nanoscale morphology of single fibers and the dispersion of CNTs within the polymer matrix. For chemical analysis, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, Nicolet iS 10, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) was applied to compare the spectra of PAA and PI, confirming the imidization process and associated changes in functional groups. To evaluate thermal stability, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA, Netzsch STA 449 F3, Germany) was employed to monitor the weight loss behavior under controlled heating, providing insights into decomposition temperatures and thermal endurance.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this paper, rather than relying on conventional geometric capacitance enhancement, the authors present a new sensing framework in which pressure-driven impedance release activates previously suppressed polarization channels, converting series resistance from a limiting factor into a controllable gain parameter, and validate this concept through temperature-invariant polyimide sensor operation and wide-temperature CNN-assisted tactile recognition. While previous studies have typically enhanced sensitivity through geometric or dielectric modulation at the expense of dynamic response, environmental stability, or operating range due to intrinsic impedance constraints, this work uniquely overcomes such limitations by formalizing an impedance-driven amplification mechanism that activates previously suppressed polarization channels, and rigorously validates the resulting simultaneous enhancement of electrical and operational performance through impedance spectroscopy, systematic pressure-dependent measurements, and theoretical analysis. The integration of well-established principles from dielectric spectroscopy, impedance analysis, and relaxation dynamics into a coherent sensing framework that redefines impedance—traditionally treated as a parasitic loss to be minimized—as an active gain knob for releasing suppressed polarization channels is quite novel.
Therefore, this paper could be further considered for publication in Nature Communications, as long as the following comments can be well addressed:
1. It would be interesting to analyze whether the observed capacitance enhancement is uniquely tied to mechanical compression or whether comparable effects can be obtained by selectively tuning the series resistance without mechanical pressure.
2. In Figures 3b and 3c, the outstanding temperature-independent performances are quite interesting. However, the statement that “… enabled by the thermally robust polyimide matrix …” in line 22 (page 12) is insufficient on its own. It would be informative to clarify whether the observed temperature robustness arises from the impedance-driven sensing mechanism itself.
3. In line 19 (page 2), the authors state that “Ionic materials are prone to leakage, evaporation, and thermal degradation.” This seems overgeneralized, as ion-confined polymer matrix systems have shown low leakage and long-term stability.
4. Given that Figure 1b (inset) suggests a millimeter-scale thickness, additional clarification of the air-jet spinning process would improve the clarity and reproducibility of the fabrication method.
5. The Introduction currently lacks sufficient citations to recent wearable/implantable tissue-like studies that are essential for establishing tissue-device conformality. I am therefore suggesting several relevant papers and would like you to incorporate them accordingly. (Nature Nanotechnology (2025) DOI https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-025-02031-x ; Nature Electronics 8, 474-484 (2025) ; Nature Electronics 7, 800 (2024) ; Nature Nanotechnology 17, 849 (2022))
6. At present, several key concepts, terms, and symbols (e.g., transition frequency, impedance release, the physical meaning of |X| evolution, and the relationship between series resistance and polarization activation) are difficult to understand from the main text alone. A reader must consult Supplementary Note 1 to follow the core mechanism, which reduces the readability of the paper. The authors should consider expanding the main text to include concise but clear explanations of these concepts.
7.Figure 2d appears to exhibit two clearly different sensing regimes at low and high pressure ranges, corresponding to different slopes. However, these results are not clearly visible in the current figure. The authors should consider annotating the extracted slopes for these two regions and adding an inset that enlarges the low-pressure area.
8. In Figure S6, the cross-sectional SEM images suggest noticeable differences in fiber thickness between the electrode layers and the dielectric layer. It is not clear whether this difference originates from variations in electrospinning conditions (e.g., solution properties or CNT loading), or whether it is an intentional design choice. In addition, the overall thickness of each layer and of the full device is not clearly specified. According to the Methods section, each layer appears to be fabricated using a 1 mL syringe over approximately 15 minutes. Based on the device photographs, the assembled sensor appears relatively thick, which raises questions about layer-to-layer thickness uniformity. Could authors report the average fiber diameter and thickness distribution for each layer, the thickness of each individual layer, and the total thickness of the assembled device.
9. In Figure 2d, devices using metallic foil electrodes show significantly inferior sensing performance compared to those with porous fiber electrodes. However, the manuscript does not clearly explain why metallic electrodes fail to provide effective sensing in this system. A more explicit explanation is needed, particularly addressing why high electrical conductivity alone is insufficient. Clarifying this point would strengthen the design rationale for porous electrodes.
10. Figures S1b and S1c suggest that ionic capacitive pressure sensors typically exhibit nF level signals, whereas the proposed impedance-based capacitive sensors operate at the μF level. However, Figure S13 shows that under an 80 kPa load, the measured capacitance change is on the order of ~25 nF. This discrepancy may give the impression that the signal magnitude is overstated. The authors should clarify the operating conditions under which μF level signals are achieved.
11. The fire-scenario demonstration effectively shows that the sensor can operate stably at elevated temperatures. However, a real fire scenario typically involves conditions beyond uniform high temperature, such as direct flame exposure, oxidation, and transient thermal gradients. The authors have any additional analysis, characterization, or testing under more extreme fire-related conditions?

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript reports an impedance-driven PI–CNT all-fiber capacitive sensor with high sensitivity, MPa-level pressure operation, and wide temperature tolerance; similar research has been reported [1–4]. These results are promising, but several scientific and methodological issues must be addressed before the work can be considered for publication in a high-impact venue.
The mechanistic validation of the proposed “impedance-release” concept remains largely qualitative. The contributions of geometric effects, dielectric response, and impedance evolution are not quantitatively separated, and alternative explanations—such as compression-induced CNT tunneling or leakage—are not rigorously excluded.[1–3] Frequency-dependent behavior, noise/drift characteristics, and device-to-device reproducibility are also insufficiently explored. In addition, the repeated reference to “real-time feedback” is not supported, as the system demonstrates sensing only.[9,10]
The finite-element analysis (FEA) relies on constitutive assumptions inconsistent with the highly porous (>90%) fiber architecture, limiting its mechanistic reliability.[2–4] Moreover, claims of universality are not substantiated because all demonstrations are restricted to a single PI–CNT platform without validation in chemically distinct systems.[2,3,5]
Finally, the evaluation of pressure mapping and the deep-learning demonstration lacks statistical rigor, controlled comparisons, and methodological transparency.[11]
Overall, the study presents a compelling device concept but currently reads as a high-performance demonstration of a single optimized system rather than a fully validated, generalizable design framework. Addressing the mechanistic, modeling, reproducibility, and benchmarking issues will substantially strengthen the manuscript.

[Additional Major Comments]
1. Mechanism not quantitatively validated; alternative explanations not excluded
Section 2.2 and Supplementary Note 1 ascribe the large observed ΔC to an “impedance‑release” mechanism, in which pressure‑induced reductions in Rs and shifts in the polarization transition frequency are proposed to dominate the response. However, the data in Fig. 2a–f and Supplementary Fig. S9 do not quantitatively disentangle the respective contributions of geometric effects, intrinsic dielectric properties, and impedance evolution.[1–4]In addition, CNT‑based composites are well known to exhibit compression‑induced tunneling and the formation of leakage pathways, both of which can manifest as an apparent increase in capacitance in porous structures.[1–3] In the present manuscript, these alternative pathways have not yet been rigorously differentiated from the proposed mechanism. A more systematic analysis is required to clarify whether the pressure dependence of Rs primarily reflects activated polarization, or whether it is instead dominated by changes in conductive pathways and leakage currents. In iontronic systems, capacitances of this magnitude are typically associated with electric‑double‑layer formation at soft interfaces,[4–8] whereas in the present non‑ionic architecture the existence of such interfacial mechanisms is not clearly established. Additional controls and quantitative checks are therefore needed to demonstrate that the observed behavior cannot be fully explained by leakage or tunneling effects.[4–8]
2. FEA does not adequately represent the highly porous architecture
In Fig. 2g,h and Supplementary Fig. S11, the FEA treats the electrode and dielectric layers as incompressible Neo‑Hookean solids with GPa‑level Young’s moduli taken from tensile tests. However, Fig. 1g and the Supplementary tables/figures (porosity > 90%) indicate that the actual structure is a PI–CNT fiber sponge exhibiting foam‑like compressive densification. Incompressible Neo‑Hookean models are generally appropriate for dense elastomeric solids, whereas open‑cell foams and fiber networks are typically described by compressible hyperelastic or foam‑type constitutive laws that explicitly capture volumetric strain and pore collapse.[2–4] Under these assumptions, the D/E/ED simulations can only be interpreted as qualitative approximations; the fact that the ED case reproduces a two‑slope C–P curve is not, by itself, a physically faithful validation of the mechanistic behavior of the porous PI–CNT architecture. At a minimum, the main text should explicitly acknowledge these limitations, and ideally the simulations should be updated using a compressible/foam‑type model calibrated to the measured compressive stress–strain response.[2–4]
3. Generality claims are not supported by evidence beyond a single PI–CNT system
The manuscript presents the proposed approach as broadly applicable to heterogeneous non‑ionic composites, yet all experimental demonstrations are confined to a single PI–CNT all‑fiber system.[1–4] Given the extensive literature on diverse polymer–filler combinations (e.g. PDMS/CNT or PDMS/graphene, MXene/polymer composites, PU/PI foams, carbon‑black or metal‑nanowire elastomers), it would be important to verify whether similar impedance‑driven trends can be reproduced in at least one chemically distinct platform in order to substantiate the notion of a “general design rule”. As currently presented, the evidence more strongly supports a system-specific optimization of PI–CNT fiber networks than with a broadly validated universal strategy.[2,3,5]
4. Claim of providing “real-time feedback” is not supported.
The manuscript repeatedly uses the term “real-time feedback,” yet the presented system demonstrates only sensing and perception via pressure mapping and CNN-based recognition, without any integrated haptic actuator or closed-loop control scheme. As currently implemented, the work constitutes a sensing-only proof-of-concept, and the terminology should be adjusted to avoid implying a closed-loop or haptic feedback–enabled system that is not implemented here.[9, 10]
5. Insufficient statistical reporting of pressure mapping patterns.
Quantitative statistical metrics should be provided to supplement Fig. 5(b), in order to demonstrate that the pressure-mapping patterns of identical objects are consistent across repeated trials. In addition, a 2D spatio-frequency analysis would allow direct comparison of the spatial–frequency characteristics among different objects. For Fig. S16, the applied pressure should be controlled and kept consistent across all comparative groups; however, the current data suggest noticeable variation. Furthermore, the reference sensors used for benchmarking differ in geometry and electrode layout, which undermines the validity of the comparisons. These factors collectively weaken the conclusions regarding recognition accuracy. For instance, both the Traditional and Impedance types exhibit poorer spatial resolution at 25 °C yet appear to perform better at 200 °C—an outcome that contradicts physical intuition and calls for additional verification. Incorporating a ground-truth reference measurement across all three sensing modalities would substantially strengthen the reliability of the comparison.
6. Deep learning demonstration lacks rigor and controlled comparison.
The dataset size is limited (300 samples), no cross-validation or train/test robustness analysis is performed, and key details—such as signal preprocessing, data normalization, construction of the 52×52 input arrays, or justification for using a 1D rather than 3D CNN architecture—are missing. The t-SNE plots indicate linearly separable clusters even for the Traditional type, yet the classification accuracy for that case drops to ~80% without sufficient explanation. Overall, the DL demonstration would benefit from clearer methodological transparency, controlled comparison, and more rigorous evaluation.[11]
[Additional minor comments]
1) Recent high-performance capacitive and iontronic sensors already achieve wide pressure ranges and high sensitivities through graded, porous, or impedance-engineered architectures.[4,6–8] While the wide temperature window and impedance-related mechanism explored here provide meaningful novelty, a more balanced and up-to-date discussion of these recent advances would help contextualize the contribution and avoid overstating the level of performance innovation.
2)Supplementary Fig. S13 reports sub-10 ms response and recovery times; however, there is no systematic investigation of loading-rate dependence, dwell-time effects, or rate-dependent hysteresis. These characteristics are particularly important for impedance-driven mechanisms and are routinely quantified in recent iontronic sensor literature.[4,6–8]
3) Although Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. S15 demonstrate functional operation from −80 to 200 °C, the study does not include repeated thermal cycling or long-term testing across extreme transitions. Temperature-dependent analyses of Rs(T,ω), tan δ(T,ω), Arrhenius-type activation behavior, and high-temperature durability would significantly strengthen claims of thermal robustness, as these analyses are standard in high-temperature iontronic sensor studies.[6–8]
4) SEM and KPFM results offer useful qualitative insights, but additional microstructure-resolved evidence—such as in-situ micro-CT, conductive-AFM, or local impedance mapping—would more convincingly validate the proposed percolation and impedance-release mechanisms.[4,6–8] Moreover, only a single KPFM region is shown; statistical distributions, multiple measurement sites, or correlations between surface potential and polarization would improve the robustness of the interpretation.
5) Porous dielectric structures generally exhibit compression–release hysteresis, but aside from long-cycle stability, no loading–unloading curves are presented. Quantifying hysteresis is essential for evaluating practical usability and mechanism consistency.
6)The reported porosity (~90%) lacks methodological detail. It is unclear whether it was determined via gravimetry, image-based analysis, mercury porosimetry, nitrogen adsorption, or another technique. Explicitly stating the measurement method is necessary for reproducibility.
7) Performance data appear to be based on single devices without error bars or batch-to-batch statistics. Given the stochastic nature of fiber spinning, CNT distribution, and gradient formation, reproducibility is essential to assess manufacturing robustness. Additionally, several parameters critical to reproducibility—such as airflow nozzle size, air temperature, humidity, and fiber diameter distribution—are not reported.

Response: We agree with the reviewer that attributing the temperature-invariant performance solely
4

therefore clarify that the observed wide-temperature stability is closely associated with the non-ionic,
impedance-driven sensing mechanism, which is fundamentally different from mechanisms
dominated by ionic transport.
To examine this distinction, we performed a controlled comparison of three capacitive pressure
sensors constructed using the same PI fiber matrix: the impedance-driven sensor (PI/CNTs),
a traditional capacitive sensor (PI), and an iontronic sensor (PI/IL). As shown in Figure R2, although
all three devices employ the thermally stable PI matrix and remain operational at elevated
temperature, their sensing behaviors differ markedly at 200 °C. The iontronic sensor exhibits early
signal saturation and pronounced temperature sensitivity, while the traditional PI sensor shows only
a limited pressure response. In contrast, the impedance-driven sensor maintains a robust and
continuous pressure-dependent signal under the same conditions.
Mechanistically, this difference arises because the impedance-driven readout relies on
electronic and interfacial polarization rather than ionic migration. Temperature variations do
influence the conductivity of the CNTs network, affecting both the baseline capacitance (C₀) and
the response magnitude (ΔC). However, in the impedance-driven system, these parameters scale
proportionally with temperature, such that the normalized response (ΔC/C₀) remains stable over a
wide temperature range. This behavior indicates that the observed temperature robustness originates
from the coupling of a thermally robust material platform (PI) with a thermally stable, impedance-
regulated electronic polarization mechanism, rather than from material stability alone.

9. In Figure 2d, devices using metallic foil electrodes show significantly inferior sensing
performance compared to those with porous fiber electrodes. However, the manuscript does
not clearly explain why metallic electrodes fail to provide effective sensing in this system. A
more explicit explanation is needed, particularly addressing why high electrical conductivity
alone is insufficient. Clarifying this point would strengthen the design rationale for porous
electrodes.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful question regarding the role of electrode
conductivity. As shown in Figure R5, the use of a metallic Cu foil electrode indeed leads to a higher
absolute capacitance due to its high electrical conductivity. However, in the impedance-driven
sensing framework proposed in this work, sensing performance is not determined by conductivity
alone, but rather by whether the electrode–dielectric interface provides sufficient and controllable
impedance modulation.
Because the Cu foil electrode presents a dense and continuous conductive surface, extensive
interfacial contact with the dielectric layer is already established in the initial state, resulting in a
high baseline capacitance (C₀). This significantly reduces the relative capacitance change (ΔC/C₀)
and limits the achievable sensitivity. In contrast, the porous fiber electrode exhibits restricted initial
contact and higher interfacial impedance, allowing polarization to be gradually activated under
applied pressure. This enables a wider dynamic modulation range of the series impedance and leads
to a more effective and stable capacitance readout.
Therefore, the inferior sensing performance of metallic foil electrodes in this system does not
arise from insufficient conductivity, but from the lack of tunable interfacial impedance space, which
is essential for impedance-regulated amplification in the proposed sensing mechanism.
Corresponding explanations and the additional comparative data have been incorporated into the
revised main text and Supplementary Information.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment regarding the relevance of fire-related
conditions. We would like to clarify that the fire-scenario demonstration presented in this work is
not intended to represent a realistic or sustainable operating condition for the sensor, but rather to
illustrate its behavior under elevated temperature prior to material degradation. The intended
working regime of the device is below the thermal stability limit of the constituent materials
(≤200 °C), where long-term and repeatable operation can be reliably maintained.
In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have additionally conducted a more extreme test
involving direct flame exposure to more closely mimic a real fire scenario. As shown in Figure R6,
after direct burning, the sensor no longer exhibits stable or repeatable sensing behavior. Instead, the
signal becomes abnormally elevated and highly unstable. This degradation is attributed to
irreversible material damage, including carbonization and disruption of the fibrous network, which
fundamentally alters the electrical pathways and impedance characteristics. These results indicate
18
that direct flame exposure exceeds the intrinsic thermal tolerance of the current PI/CNTs material
system.
Importantly, this outcome does not contradict the conclusions of this work. Rather, it highlights
the distinction between stable high-temperature operation within the material’s thermal endurance
window and extreme fire conditions that lead to material decomposition. Reliable sensing
performance in such extreme environments would require additional design strategies, such as the
incorporation of flame-resistant or ablation-resistant materials, protective coatings, or thermal
barrier layers, which are beyond the scope of the present study but represent meaningful directions
for future exploration.
Corresponding descriptions and the additional experimental results have been included in the
revised manuscript to clarify the operational boundaries and to address the reviewer’s concern.

Reviewer #2:
Comment: The manuscript reports an impedance-driven PI–CNT all-fiber capacitive sensor with
high sensitivity, MPa-level pressure operation, and wide temperature tolerance; similar research has
been reported [1–4]. These results are promising, but several scientific and methodological issues
must be addressed before the work can be considered for publication in a high-impact venue. The
20
mechanistic validation of the proposed “impedance-release” concept remains largely qualitative.
The contributions of geometric effects, dielectric response, and impedance evolution are not
quantitatively separated, and alternative explanations—such as compression-induced CNT
tunneling or leakage—are not rigorously excluded.[1–3] Frequency-dependent behavior, noise/drift
characteristics, and device-to-device reproducibility are also insufficiently explored. In addition,
the repeated reference to “real-time feedback” is not supported, as the system demonstrates
sensing only.[9,10] The finite-element analysis (FEA) relies on constitutive assumptions inconsistent
with the highly porous (>90%) fiber architecture, limiting its mechanistic reliability.[2–4] Moreover,
claims of universality are not substantiated because all demonstrations are restricted to a single PI–
CNT platform without validation in chemically distinct systems.[2,3,5] Finally, the evaluation of
pressure mapping and the deep-learning demonstration lacks statistical rigor, controlled
comparisons, and methodological transparency.[11] Overall, the study presents a compelling device
concept but currently reads as a high-performance demonstration of a single optimized system rather
than a fully validated, generalizable design framework. Addressing the mechanistic, modeling,
reproducibility, and benchmarking issues will substantially strengthen the manuscript.

Response: We thank the reviewer for the rigorous and technically well-founded critique regarding
the applicability of our finite-element analysis (FEA) to a highly porous (>90%) PI–CNTs fibrous
architecture. We therefore clarify and revise the manuscript to explicitly delimit the role and validity
of the FEA used in this work.
The simulations were not intended to reproduce the detailed mechanical behavior of the porous
PI–CNTs sponge, nor to provide a quantitative validation of the impedance-release mechanism.
Instead, the FEA serves as a trend-level, homogenized comparison between three idealized
deformation modes under identical boundary conditions—coupled deformation of electrode and
dielectric layers (E–D), deformation of the electrode layers only (E), and deformation of the
dielectric layer only (D). To avoid any implication of microstructural fidelity, we have revised the
text to emphasize that the porous architecture is treated in a homogenized manner and that the
simulations do not resolve explicit pores, fiber bending, or foam-like densification.
Within this deliberately limited framework, the purpose of the FEA is strictly comparative
rather than predictive: it illustrates that deformation of the electrode layers alone primarily alters
29
conductive pathways, deformation of the dielectric layer alone produces only a weak electrical
response, and that a pronounced amplification tendency is observed in this idealized comparison
only when deformation of electrode and dielectric layers is coupled. This qualitative comparison is
used solely to support the cooperative interpretation of electrode–dielectric deformation, and not as
a physically faithful model of the porous micromechanics or a quantitative validation of the
experimental pressure–capacitance response.
To make these assumptions and limitations unambiguous, we have revised the main text and
Supplementary Information and added a schematic illustration (Figure R9) that summarizes the
conceptual deformation modes considered in the simulations, without implying a realistic
representation of the fibrous sponge structure. We also explicitly state in the revised manuscript that
a compressible foam-type constitutive model calibrated to the measured compressive stress–strain
response would be required for quantitative mechanical modeling of the porous architecture, which
lies beyond the scope of the present study.
